# This is the (1ST)first assignment of importing statistical packages

install.packages("haven")
install.packages("DBI")
install.packages("RSQLite")
install.packages("readr")

#haven reads statistical package files like (SPSS, Stata, SAS), DBI is for the database and RSQLite is the translator for databases to make R understand it.

library(haven)             
library(DBI)               
library(RSQLite)           
library(readr) 

#I first create the folder called 'data' to store our data and then make a table called 'students'

dir.create("data")

students <- data.frame(
student_id = 1:15,
name = c("Alice","Brian","Claire","David","Emma","Felix","Grace","Henry",
              "Irene","James","Karen","Leo","Mary","Nathan","Olivia"),
gender = c("F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F"),
class = c("A","A","B","B","A","C","C","A","B","C","A","B","C","B","A"),
math = c(78,65,92,45,81,59,74,88,67,53,95,70,82,38,76),
english = c(85,58,88,52,79,63,90,76,71,49,93,66,87,44,81), 
science = c(72,70,95,48,84,55,68,91,62,58,97,73,80,41,79)
)

head(students)
tail(students)

#am saving my csv sheet from R
write.csv(students, "data/student_marks.csv", row.names = FALSE)   

#and here am saving my spss data from R too
write_sav(students, "data/student_marks.sav") 

#That's for stata if whenever I want stata data
write_dta(students, "data/student_marks.dta")  

#Whenever I want to use sql commands I have first to connect it with R and after I will disconnect it to proceed with R codes

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/school.sqlite")

if (dbExistsTable(con, "student_marks")) {
  dbExecute(con, "ALTER TABLE student_marks RENAME TO student_marks_old")
  }          #if the table exists I rename it instead of dropping it

dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE student_marks (
    student_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name       TEXT,
    gender     TEXT,
    class      TEXT,
    math       INTEGER,
    english    INTEGER,
    science    INTEGER
  )
")

dbAppendTable(con, "student_marks", students)
dbDisconnect(con)

(spss_data <- read_sav("data/student_marks.sav")) 
head(spss_data <- read_sav("data/student_marks.sav"))
str(spss_data)

(stata_data <- read_dta("data/student_marks.dta"))
str(stata_data)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/school.sqlite")

dbListTables(con)                    
dbListFields(con, "student_marks") 

db_data <- dbReadTable(con, "student_marks")

(top_students <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT name, class, math
  FROM student_marks
  WHERE math > 80
  ORDER BY math DESC
"))

head(db_data)
dbDisconnect(con)

(csv_data <- read.csv("data/student_marks.csv"))
nrow(spss_data)
nrow(stata_data)
nrow(csv_data)

#If that table name exist we are goung to build a unique backup name using today's date and time and rename it so that nothing lost

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/school.sqlite")
if (dbExistsTable(con, "student_marks")) {

  backup_name <- paste0("student_marks_old_", format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S"))
  dbExecute(con, paste0("ALTER TABLE student_marks RENAME TO ", backup_name))
}

dbDisconnect(con)

# THIS IS THE (2ND)SECOND ASSIGNMENT OF Using the geom functions

library(ggplot2)

# geom_bar(): counts rows in each category

ggplot(students, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Number of students per class", x = "Class", y = "Count")

# geom_histogram(): shows how one numeric variable is distributed

ggplot(students, aes(x = math)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "orange", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of math marks", x = "Math mark", y = "Number of students")

# geom_boxplot(): compares a number across groups

ggplot(students, aes(x = class, y = math)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen") +
  labs(title = "Math marks by class", x = "Class", y = "Math mark")
  
# geom_density(): a smooth curve showing where the math marks are concentrated

ggplot(students, aes(x = math)) +                       
  geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +         
  labs(title = "Density of math marks", x = "Math mark", y = "Density")

# geom_rug(): adds a small tick on the axis for every student

ggplot(students, aes(x = math)) +
  geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +         
  geom_rug(color = "darkblue") +                        
  labs(title = "Density of math marks with rug", x = "Math mark", y = "Density")

# geom_violin(): a density curve turned sideways and mirrored, one per class

ggplot(students, aes(x = class, y = math)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "plum") +                          
  labs(title = "Math marks by class (violin)", x = "Class", y = "Math mark")

# geom_jitter(): the actual points, shifted slightly so they don't overlap

ggplot(students, aes(x = class, y = math)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen", outlier.shape = NA) +   # box without extra outlier dots
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, color = "darkred") +  # one dot per student
  labs(title = "Math marks by class with individual students", x = "Class", y = "Math mark")
  
# geom_point() & geom_smooth(): Scatter plot with a trendline comparing math vs english
ggplot(students, aes(x = math, y = english)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", col = "red", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Math vs English Marks with Trendline", x = "Math Mark", y = "English Mark")

# geom_line(): Line plot showing math marks sequentially by student ID
ggplot(students, aes(x = student_id, y = math)) +
  geom_line(color = "maroon", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "purple", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Math Marks Progression Across Students", x = "Student ID", y = "Math Mark")

# geom_text(): Scatter plot with student names labeled next to their points
ggplot(students, aes(x = math, y = science, label = name)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Math vs Science Marks Labeled by Student Name", x = "Math Mark", y = "Science Mark")

# geom_hline() & geom_vline(): Adding reference lines (e.g., passing mark of 50)
ggplot(students, aes(x = math, y = english)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Marks with Passing Threshold Lines (50)", x = "Math Mark", y = "English Mark")

# 3RD ASSIGNMRNT IT'S FOR THE APPLY FUNCTIONS/FAMILY USAGE

# Extract just the numeric score columns for matrix/apply operations
score_matrix <- as.matrix(students[, c("math", "english", "science")])
score_df <- students[, c("math", "english", "science")]

# apply(): Apply a function across margins (e.g., find mean score for each student/row -> margin 1)
(row_means <- apply(score_matrix, 1, mean))

# lapply(): Apply a function to a list/data frame, always returns a LIST
(lapply_res <- lapply(score_df, mean))

# sapply(): Simplified version of lapply, returns a VECTOR or matrix if possible
(sapply_res <- sapply(score_df, mean))

# vapply(): Like sapply, but you explicitly specify the expected return type for safety
(vapply_res <- vapply(score_df, mean, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)))

# tapply(): Apply a function across subsets defined by a factor (e.g., mean math score BY class)
(tapply_res <- tapply(students$math, students$class, mean))

# mapply(): Multivariate apply (e.g., add math and english scores element-by-element)
(mapply_res <- mapply(function(m, e) (m + e) / 2, students$math, students$english))

# rapply(): Recursive apply for nested lists (we can wrap score_df into a list to demonstrate)
nested_list <- list(scores = score_df)
rapply_res <- rapply(nested_list, function(x) x + 2, classes = "numeric")
head(rapply_res)  

# The other question which is the last one(4th assignment) that asks to find a dataset which can fit multiple linear regression and it's interpretation

# Fit the multiple linear regression model
mlr_model <- lm(science ~ math + english, data = students)

# View the regression summary and coefficients
summary(mlr_model)

#By Predicting a student's science score based on their math and english scores. Our regression equation is equal to science = 7.22+(1.36*math)-(0.45*english)

#Math (+1.36, p < 0.001):Strong Positive Impact: Holding English constant, for every 1-point increase in a student's math mark, their science score increases by 1.36 points. 
#This relationship is highly statistically significant.English (-0.45, p = 0.002):Statistical Suppression Effect: Holding Math constant, a 1-point increase in English corresponds to a $-0.45$ point change in science. In this specific dataset, this negative coefficient arises because Math and English scores overlap heavily in explaining Science variance (multicollinearity). It is statistically significant (p = 0.002).
#Intercept (7.22, p = 0.065):Baseline Value: The theoretical starting science score if both Math and English were zero (serving as a mathematical anchor rather than a real-world student scenario

#Multiple R-squared (0.9746):Exceptional Explanatory Power: 97.46% of the total variance in science scores is explained by the combination of math and english marks.

#Adjusted R-squared (0.9704):Confirms that even after accounting for the number of predictors, the model remains robustly predictive (97.04%).

#Overall F-statistic (p = 2.68* 10^(-10):Proves that the model as a whole is overwhelmingly significant compared to a model with no predictors.

#THE LAST QUESTION ABOUT VARIABLE SELECTION METHODS

#This is the process of choosing which predictor variables are we going to include in regression model to get the best balance between accuracy and simplicity whic avoids overfitting.

#For instance:

# Start with a full model and let R perform stepwise/backward elimination
full_model <- lm(science ~ math + english, data = students)
step_model <- step(full_model, direction = "backward")

# View the summary of the optimized model selected
summary(step_model)
